title: Identity Theft Statistics 2026: What the Data Actually Shows
excerpt: Identity theft affects millions of people every year — but the numbers behind it reveal important patterns about who is targeted, how accounts get compromised, and what defenses actually work. Here's what the latest data shows and what you can do about it.
content:
The Scale of Identity Theft in 2026

Identity theft is not a niche concern. According to the FTC's Consumer Sentinel Network, over 1.4 million identity theft reports were filed in 2024 in the United States alone — and that's only the fraction reported. The FTC estimates that for every report filed, several incidents go unreported because victims don't know they've been compromised until much later.

Globally, Javelin Strategy & Research estimates that identity fraud losses in the US exceeded $23 billion in 2023. The average victim spends over 200 hours resolving identity theft — roughly five full work weeks — even when the financial loss is relatively small. That time cost doesn't account for the credit score damage, loan rejections, and psychological toll that follow many incidents.

Understanding the statistics isn't just academic. The patterns in the data reveal where the actual risk lies, and more importantly, which defenses are most effective. The following breakdown draws from the FTC, Javelin Strategy & Research, IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report, and identity protection industry data through 2025.

How Identities Get Stolen: The Real Numbers

The public often imagines identity theft as the result of sophisticated hacking — a lone attacker breaking encryption or cracking passwords. The actual data tells a different story:

  • Data breaches (35%) — The largest single source. When a company you've done business with is breached, your credentials or personal data may appear in breach databases sold on dark web marketplaces, sometimes within hours of the breach. IBM's 2024 Cost of a Data Breach Report found the average breach takes 194 days to identify and 64 days to contain.
  • Phishing and social engineering (25%) — Victims are tricked into giving up their own credentials. This includes email phishing, smishing (SMS), and phone-based vishing scams. AI-generated phishing messages have become dramatically more convincing since 2023, removing the spelling errors and awkward phrasing that made older attacks easier to spot.
  • Account takeover via credential stuffing (18%) — Attackers use credentials from one breach to access accounts on other services, exploiting password reuse. If you use the same password across multiple sites, this is your primary risk vector. Automated credential stuffing attacks can test millions of login combinations per day.
  • Physical theft and mail theft (12%) — Stolen wallets, mail, and discarded documents remain surprisingly common sources of identity theft, particularly targeting older adults. Preapproved credit card offers and financial statements are high-value mail theft targets.
  • Insider threats and other methods (10%) — Compromised employees at financial institutions, healthcare providers, and retailers. Healthcare sector breaches have increased significantly, partly due to ransomware attacks that expose patient records.

The upshot: for most people, the top threats are data breaches and credential reuse — both of which are addressed by a single behavioral change: using unique passwords for every account. See our guide on responding to a data breach if your data has already been exposed.

Who Is Most at Risk?

Identity theft affects all demographics, but the FTC's data shows important patterns:

Age 30–49 files the most identity theft reports in absolute numbers, likely because this group has the most financial accounts, credit history, and online presence. This age group typically has mortgages, investment accounts, employer benefits, and active credit cards — more entry points for fraud.

Adults 60+ face disproportionate losses per incident — the FTC found that older adults lose significantly more per identity theft event, partly because they're more often targeted by phone-based scams and less likely to monitor accounts for suspicious activity. In 2024, adults 70 and older reported a median loss of $800 per fraud incident, compared to $200 for those ages 18–29.

Children are increasingly targeted because their clean credit history goes unmonitored for years. Child identity theft often goes undiscovered until the victim applies for credit as a young adult and finds accounts in their name dating back to childhood. Some estimates suggest over 1 million children are victims of identity fraud each year in the US.

Military personnel and veterans are disproportionately represented in identity theft reports, partly because frequent moves and deployments make it harder to monitor accounts consistently. Soldiers deployed overseas are particularly vulnerable because they can't respond quickly to suspicious account activity.

Recent data breach victims face a 6x higher risk of identity theft in the 12 months following a breach notification, according to Javelin research. This is why acting quickly after receiving a breach notification is critical.

The Most Common Types of Identity Fraud

Not all identity theft leads to the same outcome. The FTC's 2024 data breaks down the most common fraud categories:

  • Government benefits fraud (24%) — Fraudulent tax returns (claiming someone else's refund), unemployment claims, and Social Security benefit theft. COVID-era fraud programs created a wave of government benefits fraud that remains elevated. Tax identity theft alone resulted in over $5.5 billion in fraudulent refunds in recent filing years.
  • Credit card fraud (18%) — Opening new credit cards in the victim's name, or using compromised card numbers for fraudulent purchases. New account credit card fraud is more damaging than existing account fraud because it creates negative payment history in the victim's credit file.
  • Loan and lease fraud (15%) — Fraudulent applications for personal loans, auto loans, and apartment leases. These are particularly damaging because the resulting hard inquiries and negative payment records can affect the victim's credit score for 7 years.
  • Bank account fraud (12%) — Unauthorized access to existing bank accounts, or opening new accounts in the victim's name to receive or launder stolen funds. Zelle and Venmo fraud has increased dramatically, with funds often irretrievable once transferred.
  • Utilities fraud (8%) — Opening utilities accounts (electricity, cable, phone) in the victim's name to avoid paying deposits. These accounts often go to collections before the victim discovers the fraud.
  • Medical identity theft (5%) — Using someone's insurance or identity to obtain medical treatment or prescription drugs. This can result in incorrect medical records that create genuine treatment risks.

Dark Web Markets: Where Stolen Data Goes

After a data breach, stolen credentials don't sit unused. They're typically sold in batches on dark web marketplaces within days of the breach. Prices vary dramatically by data type:

  • Email/password combinations: $0.50–$5 per record (in bulk)
  • Full identity packages ("fullz" — name, SSN, DOB, address): $15–$40
  • Healthcare records: $100–$1,000 (high value due to insurance fraud potential)
  • Financial account with verified balance: $25–$250+ depending on balance
  • Passport scans: $1,000–$2,000 on premium marketplaces
  • Valid credit card with CVV: $5–$20 per card, depending on credit limit and country

The Recovery Timeline: What Victims Actually Face

Recovery from identity theft is rarely quick. The FTC's data on resolution timelines shows:

  • Simple account fraud (a single fraudulent charge on an existing account): typically resolved in 1–4 weeks with the financial institution's fraud team
  • New account fraud: 6 months to 2 years to fully clear the fraudulent accounts from credit reports and restore score to pre-fraud levels
  • Tax identity theft: 6–18 months for IRS resolution; the IRS Identity Protection PIN program significantly speeds this up for future years
  • Medical identity theft: 1–3 years to correct records, often requiring direct contact with healthcare providers, insurers, and medical record clearinghouses
  • Government benefits fraud: highly variable; SSA fraud can take years to resolve if benefits are incorrectly reduced or denied

Beyond direct financial losses, 23% of identity theft victims report significant emotional distress, and 17% report that the incident affected their employment or housing prospects due to credit damage. The emotional cost of monitoring your credit and contesting fraudulent accounts for months or years is significant and rarely captured in financial statistics.

Financial and Time Costs to Victims

The financial damage from identity theft varies widely by type:

  • Credit card fraud: Average loss of $500–$1,200. Most major card networks provide $0 fraud liability for disputed charges, but recouping losses requires time and follow-up.
  • New account fraud: Average loss of $1,600–$3,000. More damaging because it damages credit history in addition to direct financial loss.
  • Tax identity theft: Direct financial loss varies, but IRS resolution takes an average of 6–9 months and requires extensive documentation. The IRS issued over $5.5 billion in fraudulent refunds before catching errors in recent years.
  • Medical identity theft: Among the most damaging — fraudulent medical claims can result in incorrect entries in your medical records and insurance coverage issues that take years to untangle. Average out-of-pocket cost to victims: $13,500.

Total annual cost to US consumers from identity theft and fraud exceeds $43 billion when accounting for direct losses, recovery costs, and lost productivity. That figure doesn't include the $200+ billion in costs to businesses, payment processors, and insurers who ultimately absorb fraud losses.

What the Data Says Actually Works

Several interventions have strong evidence behind them:

Unique passwords for every account eliminates credential stuffing attacks entirely. If a breach exposes your password from one service, it can't be used to access your other accounts. A password manager like NordPass or 1Password makes this effortless — use our free password generator to create strong, unique passwords and save them securely.

Credit freezes are the most underused protection against new account fraud. A freeze prevents anyone — including you — from opening new credit accounts in your name without a PIN. Freezing at all three bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) is free, takes about 15 minutes online, and can be temporarily lifted when you need to apply for credit. Our guide to freezing your credit walks through the process step by step.

Two-factor authentication significantly reduces account takeover risk. Even if an attacker has your password, phishing-resistant 2FA (hardware keys or passkeys) prevents login. App-based 2FA (Google Authenticator, Authy) is significantly stronger than SMS-based 2FA, which is vulnerable to SIM swapping. See our 2FA guide for setup instructions across major platforms.

Dark web monitoring with rapid response — changing passwords and freezing credit immediately after an alert — limits the window attackers have to exploit stolen data. Services like NordProtect pair monitoring with identity theft insurance and restoration support, so you have professional help if you do become a victim.

IRS Identity Protection PIN — if you've ever been a tax fraud victim, or want to prevent it proactively, the IRS allows anyone to opt in to an IP PIN program. With an IP PIN, no tax return can be filed under your SSN without that PIN. This effectively eliminates tax identity theft for enrolled taxpayers.
